headline: Stellwagen Edge in 140 feet: cod on the gravel, haddock holding the mud line
subhead: Big Harvest Moon tides scrubbed the Bank hard this week, but the bottom bite held steady while the tuna stayed scattered on bait.
body_markdown:
Start with the number that matters: 140 feet on the Stellwagen Edge, gravel bottom, water still holding in the low 50s down deep even as the surface has started sliding with these longer nights. That's where the cod have been sitting all week, and that's where the fleet has been putting its time. The Harvest Moon tides that peaked mid-week ran hard — bigger swings than we've seen in a month — and that current sweeping across the gravel humps on the southwest corner of the Bank kept sand eels and small bait pinned tight to structure. Cod don't need much of an invitation when the current's moving bait for them.

Haddock have been the more consistent producer, though, and that's not a surprise this time of year. Stellwagen Basin in 180 to 210 feet has the soft mud bottom haddock like, and boats working there with clam bait and diamond jigs tipped with squid strips have been finding steady action — not a bury-the-rail bite, but a reliable one. Fish in the 18 to 22 inch class, some bigger mixed in, coming two and three at a time on double-hook rigs when the drift lines up right. The key this week has been fishing the slower tide stages. With the moon pushing extra water, the peak of the flood and ebb on the Basin has been running too hard to hold bottom without going to serious lead. Boats that timed their drifts around the tide change did better than boats that fought the current all day.

On the tuna side, it's been a scattered week, and there's no point dressing that up. We flagged this last week — said the pattern up here would run slower and more classic than the warm-water anomalies showing up closer to the Cape — and that's exactly how it's played out. Stellwagen Bank itself has had bluefin around, but they're tracking whales and bait balls rather than sitting on any one piece of structure. When the humpbacks and finbacks have been working sand eels and mackerel schools up on top in 80 to 100 feet, especially along the northern edge toward Tillies Bank, the tuna have shown up behind them. But it's not a pattern you can set your watch to. Boats have gotten shots — jigging vertical off marks under working birds, or trolling small spreader bars and cedar plugs around bait showers — but for every good pop-up window there have been a couple hours of dead water in between.

Carter Canyon and the approach edges out toward Cape Cod Tails have had a little more consistency for anyone willing to run the extra miles. The temperature break out there has held tighter than it has closer in, and that's kept some bait stacked on the edge. Trolling spreads with ballyhoo and small tuna feathers have picked up a few school-size bluefin in the 40 to 60 inch class working that line, though it's still very much a search-and-find operation rather than a sit-and-wait bite. Anybody heading that direction should plan on burning fuel looking for birds, temp breaks, and bait before committing to a spot.

Mackerel have been thinner on the Bank than you'd want this late in September, and that's part of why the bluefin pattern has stayed loose. When the mackerel schools are thick and the bluefin are locked onto them, you get that classic surface-feeding show right on top of Stellwagen where you can run and gun all day. This week that show hasn't materialized consistently — more small, mixed bait balls than big solid mackerel schools, which spreads the tuna out instead of concentrating them.

Looking at the next few days, the moon is starting to ease off its full push, and that should settle the current back down on both the gravel and the mud. That's good news for the groundfish crowd — steadier drifts mean better bottom contact, and cod on the Edge should keep feeding as long as that gravel stays current-swept without being current-blasted. If you're targeting haddock, the Basin in 190 to 200 feet on the slower half of the tide is still the play, clam bait or squid on a standard cod rig, moving slow and covering ground until you find the pod.

For tuna, the realistic approach right now is patience and mobility rather than committing to one spot. If the whales stay working on top of the Bank, that's where to start — glass the horizon for blows and bird activity before running anywhere else. If that dries up, the edge out toward Carter Canyon and Cape Cod Tails is worth the run on a calm day, trolling small and watching the temp gauge for any break. As we roll toward the end of September, expect the classic fall transition to keep building — cod and haddock settling deeper and more predictably as the water cools, while the tuna window narrows and gets more dependent on catching that bait and those whales in the right place at the right time. Worth checking conditions closely before making the long run offshore; the bottom bite is the surer thing right now.
